notes.meaning: Moses warned the whole assembly to step back from the tents of the rebels and touch none of their property. Everything belonging to these men was set apart for complete destruction because of their sin. If the people touched anything, they would share in the rebels' punishment.

The people quickly obeyed and backed away from the tents of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram. Meanwhile, Dathan and Abiram walked outside and stood boldly at their tent entrances with their wives and children. Their stance showed open defiance and stubborn pride, without any fear of God.

Moses told the crowd that an upcoming sign would prove his mission came from God. He had not appointed himself, led the people out of Egypt, or set up the priesthood by his own choice. God Himself was about to confirm that Moses was carrying out the Lord's orders.

Moses set up a clear test between a normal death and a divine judgment. If these rebels died of old age or ordinary sickness, the people could conclude that Moses was an impostor. But if the Lord did something brand-new and the earth swallowed them alive into Sheol, the place of the dead, everyone would know they had treated God with contempt.

The moment Moses stopped speaking, the ground cracked open directly beneath the rebels. The earth swallowed Dathan, Abiram, their families, and Korah's followers along with all their belongings, and then closed back up over them. They vanished completely from the assembly in a sudden, supernatural judgment.

Hearing the terrifying cries of the sinking households, all the Israelites standing nearby fled in panic. They ran because they feared the ground might open wider and swallow them as well. Their fear showed that they recognized God's terrible power, even though their hearts were not yet truly changed.

At that same moment, fire blazed out from the Lord's presence at the tabernacle and consumed the 250 men burning incense. Because they had wrongfully claimed the right of priests, God judged them with the very element they were trying to offer. This made a clear distinction between God's chosen priests and those who rebelled.

The Lord instructed Moses to have Eleazar the priest collect the bronze incense burners from the ashes and scatter the burning coals far away. Even though the men had sinned and lost their lives, the bronze tools were holy because they had been presented before God. Eleazar was to hammer the metal into flat plates to cover the altar as an enduring sign of warning.

Eleazar gathered the bronze burners from the men who had died and had them hammered into an outer covering for the altar. This shiny bronze served as a daily visual reminder to all of Israel. It warned that no one outside the family of Aaron should ever dare to offer incense before the Lord, lest they suffer Korah's fate.

The very next morning, the entire community grumbled against Moses and Aaron, blaming them for the deaths of the rebels. They even called the rebels 'the Lord's people,' accusing God's appointed leaders of murder. This showed the stubborn blindness of the people, who refused to accept God's righteous judgment even after seeing it.

As the angry crowd gathered against Moses and Aaron, the two leaders turned toward the Tent of Meeting for refuge. The sacred cloud suddenly covered the tent, and the bright glory of the Lord appeared to defend His servants. Moses and Aaron then came to the front of the tent to hear what God would say.

God commanded Moses and Aaron to pull away from the crowd so He could destroy the whole nation in an instant. Instead of thinking of their own safety, Moses and Aaron fell facedown in humble prayer. They begged God for mercy on behalf of the very people who had just threatened them.

Moses saw that the Lord's anger had already broken out as a deadly plague among the people. He told Aaron to take holy fire from the altar, put incense in his censer, and run quickly into the crowd to make atonement. Atonement here means turning away God's wrath and restoring peace so that the people would not all die.

Aaron obeyed Moses at once, taking the censer and running straight into the middle of the dying crowd. He put on the incense, made atonement, and stood firmly between those who had died and those who were still alive. Because of his priestly intercession, the plague stopped right there.

Despite Aaron's quick action, 14,700 Israelites died from the sudden plague. This death toll did not include those who had perished the day before in the earthquake and the fire. It showed the high and tragic cost of persisting in rebellion against the Lord.

Once the plague was completely halted, Aaron walked back to Moses at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting. His faithful service as high priest had turned away God's wrath and preserved the nation. With the disaster ended, peace and proper order returned to the camp.
